The Distillery

Wild by
Design

We built a distillery in the least convenient place possible — three miles from the nearest town, at the end of an unpaved track, on the edge of one of the world's largest blanket bogs. It was the only honest choice.

Our Story

A distillery
at the edge

In 2009, Miriam Gault left a position as a senior perfumer at a large Paris fragrance house with a conviction she could not quite articulate: that the botanical materials she had access to were not the interesting ones. The interesting ones were in places nobody was looking.

She drove north. She drove further north. She stopped in Caithness — the most northerly county of the Scottish mainland, a vast flat plateau of ancient bog and shore — because the car needed petrol and the light at 9 p.m. in June was doing something she had never seen before.

She called her friend and collaborator Alasdair Finch, a distiller of whisky who had been looking for a reason to leave the industry for years. He arrived three weeks later. They found a disused farm building with a sound roof, a spring-fed burn running alongside, and a planning authority that, to their surprise, approved their application in seven months.

The first fragrance — Sphagnum — was distilled in a borrowed copper pot still in the winter of 2011. They made forty bottles. They gave most of them away.

Copper Pot Still · Caithness Distillery

The People

The Founders

M.

Miriam Gault

Head Perfumer & Co-Founder

Miriam trained at ISIPCA in Versailles and spent eleven years as a perfumer at a Paris fragrance house before leaving to pursue botanical work. She holds a BSc in Ethnobotany from Edinburgh and is a Fellow of the Perfumers' Society. She has been documenting the olfactory flora of northern Scotland for fifteen years and considers herself a very slow writer. Her forthcoming book, The Smell of Latitude, has been forthcoming for six years.

A.

Alasdair Finch

Master Distiller & Co-Founder

Alasdair spent seventeen years as a distiller with three Speyside whisky producers before joining Miriam in Caithness. He rebuilt the original farm distillery with his own hands — the copper still was sourced from a closed distillery in Orkney and modified over two winters. He is responsible for all production, sourcing, and the peculiar quarterly newsletter that has, somehow, twelve thousand subscribers. He does not have a mobile phone.

The Craft

How we
distil

01

Wild Sourcing

We harvest botanical materials on foot, at the correct season, from documented locations across Caithness and Sutherland. Nothing is farmed. Some species we have harvested from the same site for fifteen years.

02

Copper Distillation

Materials are distilled in our 200-litre copper pot still using spring water from our own burn. We run slowly — a full distillation takes twelve to sixteen hours. Speed destroys nuance.

03

Cold Maturation

Raw distillates rest in cool, dark conditions for six to eighteen months before blending. The northern climate does not hurry this. Neither do we. We have tried.

04

Hand Bottling

Each fragrance is bottled, labelled, and sealed by hand in an edition of three hundred. Every bottle bears a number. When the edition is gone, it is gone until we distil again — which may be some time.

"Come in October, when the bog
turns copper and rust.
Bring your own boots."

— Alasdair Finch
